pass_rule: all core questions substantially correct in the learner's own words, with the exercise's own numbers cited where the question asks for evidence; stretch questions inform the grade, not the gate

questions.prompt: Explain tri-color marking in your own words, then tell me what goes wrong if the collector marks concurrently with no write barrier. What does Go trade away to keep pauses short?
expected_points: white = unproven, grey = reachable but unscanned (work queue), black = scanned; roots are stacks/globals/registers; whatever is still white at the end is swept
concurrent mutation can hide a white object behind an already-black object, so it gets swept while live — a use-after-free
the write barrier hooks pointer writes during a cycle so no black-to-white edge goes unnoticed
the price is throughput: write barriers, mark assists, ~25% of GOMAXPROCS on background marking — spent to keep stop-the-world phases sub-millisecond
the STW phases are only mark setup (turning the write barrier on) and mark termination, not the whole mark — even stack scanning happens concurrently, one goroutine at a time

questions.prompt: What exactly does GOGC control? Using your own gcdemo numbers, predict what happens to GC cycle count and peak memory if you go from GOGC=100 to GOGC=400, and say which resource you are spending.
expected_points: heap goal = live heap after last cycle x (1 + GOGC/100); default 100 means collect at twice the live set
raising GOGC means rarer cycles: less CPU spent collecting, more memory held (their numbers should show roughly 19 cycles -> 5 and the goal moving to ~5x live)
lowering it is the mirror image: more CPU, less memory
GOGC changes only the slack above the live set, not the live set itself
same control in code via debug.SetGCPercent

questions.prompt: When would you set GOMEMLIMIT, and what does it do that GOGC cannot? Why did your GOGC=off run still collect — and collect more often than the default?
expected_points: GOGC is relative to the live set, so a growing live set walks the heap goal past a container limit
GOMEMLIMIT is an absolute soft limit on total runtime-managed memory (heap + stacks + runtime metadata), engaged as the total approaches it
typical use: keep GOGC=100 and set GOMEMLIMIT just under the container limit as a backstop, leaving headroom for non-Go memory
with GOGC=off the limit becomes the only pacing signal, so the runtime collects near the ceiling — in gcdemo that ceiling (100MiB) is tighter than the default 2x goal, hence more cycles
it is soft on purpose: an overshoot degrades (GC capped at 50% CPU) instead of OOM-killing; it is not a leak fix

questions.prompt: How did you measure the effect of each fix, and what did the numbers do? Why does this lesson gate on allocs/op rather than ns/op?
expected_points: go test -bench=. -benchmem -run='^$' reports allocs/op and B/op; run it without -race
cites their own before/after: ~2054 -> 1 for FormatEvents, ~13 -> 1 for EventIDs, ~2060 -> ~0 for WriteEvents
testing.AllocsPerRun gives a deterministic allocation count the automated tests can assert on
times vary with machine load and are distorted several-fold by the race detector; allocation counts are stable and point at a specific mistake

questions.prompt: Walk me through the three fixes: what was each function doing wrong, and why did the change help? Include why WriteEvents needed a sync.Pool rather than one package-level buffer.
expected_points: FormatEvents: s += x allocates a new string per iteration and copies everything so far; strings.Builder plus Grow (after summing lengths) makes it one allocation
EventIDs: append to a nil slice re-grows and re-copies about log2(n) times; make([]int64, 0, len(events)) is one allocation
WriteEvents: a temporary line string per event plus a scratch buffer built and discarded per call; write the pieces straight into a pooled buffer
sync.Pool is per-P and safe for concurrent use; one shared buffer would be a data race and would interleave output — TestWriteEventsConcurrent under -race catches it
pool contract: Reset before use, defer Put, New must be able to rebuild, contents can vanish at any GC

questions.prompt: Why does the mark phase care more about pointers than about bytes? Give a concrete representation change that reduces mark cost without storing less data.
expected_points: marking follows pointer slots in live objects; a pointer-free object lives in a noscan span and its contents are skipped entirely
a 1 MB []byte is one pointer to scan; a million-node pointer structure is a million objects to visit, in cache-hostile order
concrete: []Item instead of []*Item, indices into a value slice instead of pointers, one backing array instead of many small nodes
hidden pointers: strings, slices, maps, interfaces, funcs, and types like time.Time (*Location) make a struct scannable

questions.prompt: WriteEvents can reach zero allocations per call, but FormatEvents bottoms out at one. Why — and what would you have to change to get FormatEvents to zero?
expected_points: FormatEvents returns a fresh string the caller keeps, so the result must be heap-allocated — the allocation is part of the API
WriteEvents only needs scratch space nobody retains, which is exactly what a pool recycles
to reach zero you must change the signature: write to a caller-supplied io.Writer or append into a caller-supplied buffer
shows the general rule: allocation is often a design decision, not an implementation detail

questions.prompt: A service is being OOM-killed in a 512 MiB container. What do you look at before touching any knob, and what would make you reach for GOMEMLIMIT versus a code change?
expected_points: measure first: is the live set genuinely large (mark cost, possibly a leak) or is it high allocation rate with a small live set?
gctrace or runtime metrics show live-after-sweep versus goal; a heap profile shows which call sites hold the bytes
GOMEMLIMIT below the container limit is the right backstop against the kill, and buys time — it does not fix a leak, it turns a crash into a CPU-burning slowdown
a growing live set needs a code or retention fix; high churn over a small live set is a pooling/preallocation problem
